stories.title: How a 95 percent drop in Hormuz traffic changed global shipping
stories.summary: A crisis in one narrow passage has disrupted an industry that carries about 80 percent of the world’s trade. Six months into the United States-Israel war on Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to drive one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades. Traffic through the 33km (21-mile) chokepoint has fallen from more than 100 vessels a day to just five, disrupting the flow of oil, gas and goods worldwide. Al Jazeera visualises how a crisis in one narrow passage has disrupted an industry that carries about 80 percent of the world’s trade. Almost everything people buy, from the fuel in their cars to the grain in their bread, has likely spent time on board a vessel at sea. About 80 percent of world trade by volume moves by sea at some point, making maritime shipping essential to the global economy, according to UNCTAD, the UN’s trade and development body. Not all ships are created equal. Different vessels are built for various purposes, from moving oil to the goods we rely on every day. Oil tankers are among the largest ships and carry energy products such as crude oil, refined petroleum, and chemicals. Most crude oil is transported by Very Large Crude Carriers, or VLCCs, which can access a wide range of ports and carry about two million barrels of crude. Container ships transport consumer goods such as phones and clothing in stacked steel boxes known as containers. Some are enormous, measuring more than 400m (1,312 feet) long and carrying more than 20,000 containers.

stories.title: Iran to allow no military ships in Hormuz under potential deal with Oman
stories.summary: The latest development comes amid US President Donald Trump's threat to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way," as his administration opposes parts of the evolving agreement. Iran and Oman have reached a potential agreement to manage ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, excluding military vessels from the vital waterway. Tehran will allow military ships to transit through the Strait of Hormuz under the agreement that the Islamic Republic is negotiating with Oman, Iran’s deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday. The two countries' top diplomats met to discuss managing commercial shipping traffic in Hormuz, which remained largely shut down nearly six months after the Iran war began. Gharibabadi told state television late Tuesday that commercial shipping traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s waters. He said the routes would be temporary and that Iran and Oman must discuss a permanent maritime traffic plan within 30 to 60 days. The latest development comes amid US President Donald Trump's threat to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way", as his administration opposes parts of the evolving deal. The Trump administration has told Oman it opposes parts of the yet-to-be-announced deal, including joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route from the passage critical to global supplies of oil and natural gas. On Wednesday, Trump said he believes the US is “winning very big” as the conflict with Iran nears the six-month mark. “I have no time schedule, whatever it takes,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera. In another interview Wednesday, Trump said he thinks Iran’s Ayatollah Motjaba Khamenei is “very seriously wounded", but not dead. Motjaba Khamenei became supreme leader after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war in late February.

stories.title: Nepal floods leave 644 tourists missing, authorities say
stories.summary: The report lists eight Russians among the missing
article_sentences: NEW DELHI, August 27.
A total of 644 tourists, including eight Russians, are missing following floods in Nepal, the country’s Tourism Board said.
"Preliminary data from trekking and travel companies show that 644 travelers, including 127 Nepalese nationals, are missing in the affected area," the board said in a report.
The report lists eight Russians among the missing.
It also lists 178 Indians, 65 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians and 25 Canadians.
In total, the list includes people from 33 countries.
